opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the main concern is that people are attributing to these systems a kind of understanding that they may not actually have. When you interact with ChatGPT, it produces text that is fluent, grammatical, often quite sensible, and our natural instinct as human beings is to assume that behind fluent language there's a mind that understands what it's saying, that has a model of the world, that has goals and beliefs. That's what has always been true of language for us: if something talks to you coherently, it's another person.

But these systems are trained to predict the next word, given an enormous amount of text. And the result is something that can mimic the surface patterns of human communication extraordinarily well, without our having any real idea of what's going on inside. We don't know whether it has a consistent internal model of the world. In fact, there's a fair amount of evidence that it often doesn't. It will confidently assert things that are false, it will contradict itself from one sentence to the next, it will fail at fairly simple arithmetic or logical reasoning in ways that suggest it isn't really reasoning the way we would.

So one risk is very practical: people will trust it in situations where they shouldn't. They'll take medical advice, legal advice, factual claims at face value, because it sounds authoritative. And it isn't designed to be truthful; it's designed to be plausible.

The second concern is more about the trajectory of the field. If people believe that we're basically almost there, that we just need to scale these systems up and general intelligence will pop out, then I think that leads to a kind of complacency about the very hard questions: how do you actually get a system to reason, to plan over long time horizons, to know what it doesn't know? And crucially, how do you ensure that a system that's more capable than us remains under our control? Those questions don't get answered by making the language model bigger.

And the third thing, which honestly worries me, is that we've deployed these systems to hundreds of millions of people without really understanding how they work. We've been doing that with black boxes. In any other engineering discipline, if you built a nuclear power plant and said, "Well, we don't really know how it works, but it seems to produce electricity most of the time," nobody would let you switch it on. So overinterpreting their capabilities, in either direction, is a symptom of the fact that we just don't understand them, and that's the thing I'd like us to fix.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that ChatGPT is a remarkable piece of engineering, and I don't want to take anything away from that. But what worries me is that people look at the fluency of the output and immediately assume there's a mind behind it that resembles their own. When a system produces grammatical, confident, well-organized paragraphs, we instinctively attribute to it the kind of understanding that a human would need in order to produce the same text. And that inference is simply not warranted.

What these systems are actually doing, at the core, is predicting the next word, or the next token, based on enormous amounts of human-generated text. It turns out that when you do that at sufficient scale, you get something that looks astonishingly like intelligent conversation. But "looks like" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. The system has no stable model of the world. It has no beliefs, in the sense that it doesn't have a representation of what's true that it's committed to. It will tell you one thing, and if you push back, it will cheerfully tell you the opposite. It will invent citations, invent court cases, invent biographical details, because it has no mechanism for distinguishing what it knows from what merely sounds plausible.

So the first concern is a practical one. If people treat it as an oracle, as a reliable source of facts or advice, they are going to be misled, sometimes in ways that matter a great deal. We've already seen lawyers submit briefs full of fabricated precedents. That's a harmless example, in a sense, because it got caught. The ones that don't get caught are more worrying.

The second concern is more about the public and policy conversation. There's a tendency now to say, well, if ChatGPT can do this, then AGI must be just around the corner, we just need to make it bigger. And I think that's a mistake in both directions. It leads some people to panic about capabilities that aren't there yet, and it leads others to dismiss the whole safety question because they can see that ChatGPT isn't really thinking. Both of those reactions miss the point. We don't actually understand how these systems work internally. We don't know what they've learned, we can't predict what they'll do in new situations, and we have no reliable way to control their behavior beyond trial and error on the outputs. That should concern us whether or not you want to call it intelligent.

And I suppose the deeper issue is that fluency is precisely the thing that evolution has trained us to use as a signal of a competent, trustworthy agent. So we're uniquely badly equipped to evaluate a system whose one great strength is fluency. That's a vulnerability, and I think we should be honest about it rather than pretending we're immune to it.

astra-6.text:
What concerns me is that fluency is very easy to mistake for understanding. You ask a question, and you get a beautifully written, confident answer. Naturally, you attribute to the system the sort of knowledge and reasoning that would enable a human to give that answer. But the answer may be completely fabricated, and the system can present it with exactly the same confidence as something that is correct.

That doesn’t mean its capabilities aren’t impressive. They are. But we need to distinguish what we’ve actually demonstrated from what we infer because it sounds like a person. If people start relying on these systems for consequential decisions simply because they’re persuasive, then errors become much more serious. The ability to produce convincing language is not, by itself, a guarantee of reliability.

sol-6.1.text:
What concerns me is that fluency is very easily mistaken for understanding. You ask a question, and you get a beautifully written, confident answer. Naturally, you assume there’s some reliable process behind it—that the system knows what it’s talking about. But it can produce something completely false in exactly the same tone.

That creates a problem of trust. If you don’t already know the answer, you may have no way of telling whether what you’re reading is correct. And as people start relying on these systems for consequential decisions, that gap between how competent they appear and how reliable they actually are becomes very important.

That doesn’t mean the capabilities aren’t impressive. They are. But we need to distinguish producing convincing language from having the kind of understanding and reliability that would justify handing over responsibility.
